summaries.example: Imagine the sentence “Every student is every student.” It might mean that each student is the same as themself. But it might also sound as if all students are one single person. The puzzle comes from using “every” in two different ways. Richard’s method would look at both meanings and explain why the sentence can seem both right and wrong.
summaries.summary: Richard the Sophister was a medieval English thinker who wrote Abstractiones, a collection of more than three hundred logic puzzles called sophisms. These puzzles used short sentences that could be confusing because words like “all,” “every,” “or,” and “not” might work in different ways. Richard’s book was probably used to teach students how to find reasoning mistakes. For each puzzle, he could present a sentence, reasons supporting it, reasons rejecting it, and a solution explaining the confusion. One simple puzzle says, “Every man is every man.” It seems true if “every man” means each person separately, but false if it means all men taken together. The book became known in medieval schools, although the author’s exact identity remains uncertain. Researchers have suggested several possible Richards, but the evidence does not settle the question.
key_ideas: Richard the Sophister was an English thinker and teacher of logic connected with Oxford in the 1200s.
His book Abstractiones collected more than three hundred tricky sentences for students to study.
The puzzles often depended on words such as “all,” “every,” “or,” “if,” and “not.”
Richard usually showed arguments for a sentence, arguments against it, and then the mistake or word-confusion that explained the puzzle.
Scholars still do not know for certain which Richard wrote the book.
summaries.why_it_matters: Richard’s work shows that careful thinking is not only about knowing facts. It is also about noticing how words are being used. A sentence may seem clear until we ask exactly what each word means. Studying these old puzzles can help readers become more careful when they listen, speak, read, and decide whether an argument makes sense.

important_terms.definition: A sentence or argument that seems puzzling because a word or sentence structure can be understood in more than one way.
A person who studies and explains how reasoning works. In Richard’s time, “sophista” meant logician.
A word such as “all,” “or,” “not,” or “if” that helps connect or change the meaning of a sentence.
A mistake in reasoning caused by confusing two meanings of a word or sentence.

questions_to_think_about: Can one sentence have two meanings even when its words stay the same?
Why is it useful to study an argument that contains a mistake?
How could you rewrite “Every student is every student” to make its meaning clear?
What evidence would help historians identify the author of an old book?

summaries.example: Consider the sentence “Every man is every man.” A supporting argument can treat the subject phrase as referring to each individual person: each man is identical with himself. A rejecting argument can treat “every man” as referring to humanity taken as a whole, so that it is false that one man is all men. Richard’s solution is not simply that one side forgot a fact. Rather, the expression changes its reference within the sentence. The apparent contradiction is produced by equivocation.
summaries.summary: Richard the Sophister was an English philosopher and logician associated with Oxford during the second quarter of the thirteenth century. His principal work, Abstractiones, is a compact collection of over three hundred sophisms: sentences designed to reveal difficulties in logical analysis. Their puzzles frequently involve syncategorematic terms, whose contribution to a proposition depends on context and structure. Examples concern quantifiers, negation, conditionals, exceptions, modality, and verbs such as “begins” and “ceases.” Richard’s procedure resembles a medieval disputation. He states a sophism, sometimes within a casus, gives considerations establishing its truth, gives considerations establishing its falsity, and then explains the fallacy. In the opening example, “Every man is every man,” the phrase “every man” shifts between a distributive reading—each man individually—and a collective reading—men considered as a whole. The conflict is therefore an equivocation rather than a straightforward contradiction. The work was used as a teaching resource and survives in seven known manuscripts, two complete and five fragmentary or derivative. Its author cannot be securely identified. Proposed identifications with Fishacre, Fitz-Ralph, or Rufus rely on chronology, terminology, or doctrinal comparison, but the available evidence does not establish any of them.
key_ideas: Abstractiones was probably composed in the 1230s or 1240s and circulated in medieval universities from the late thirteenth into the fourteenth century.
Its sophisms involve semantic ambiguity, syntactic ambiguity, and distinctions in the scope or function of logical expressions.
Richard’s typical treatment moves from the proposed sophism to arguments for and against it, then to a resolution identifying the fallacy.
The collection includes standard fallacies associated with Aristotle, such as equivocation, amphiboly, and confusion between composite and divided senses.
Seven manuscripts are known, but only two are complete; the survival of derivative texts and later references suggests that the work was influential.
Richard’s identity is disputed. Suggestions include Richard Fishacre, Richard Fitz-Ralph, and Richard Rufus, but the entry does not regard the evidence as conclusive.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry demonstrates how medieval logic examined ordinary language with remarkable precision. It also illustrates a broader historical lesson: identifying an author requires more than finding a shared word or idea. Manuscript evidence, dates, terminology, and doctrines must be compared, and apparent similarities may not establish identity. Richard’s collection matters both as a record of medieval logical teaching and as a sustained study of how ambiguity can make arguments appear stronger or weaker than they are.

important_terms.definition: A logically puzzling sentence studied by medieval logicians, often because its wording permits competing interpretations or exposes a reasoning error.
A medieval term for a logician; Richard the Sophister is also called the Master of Abstractions in connection with his work.
Words whose logical function affects a whole proposition, including terms such as “all,” “or,” “if,” “not,” “necessary,” and “possible.”
A fallacy produced when the same expression is used with different meanings in an argument.
A medieval classroom exercise or situation that supplied the setting in which a sophism was to be argued and resolved.
A formal classroom debate in which a claim could be defended, challenged, and resolved through arguments.
A collection titled Abstractiones that summarizes more than three hundred sophisms and was likely used as a logical teaching text.

questions_to_think_about: When does ambiguity belong to a word’s meaning, and when does it arise from sentence structure?
Does a successful proof of a sentence show that the sentence is true, or might it show only that one reading is true?
Why would a medieval teacher present both a proof and a disproof before giving a resolution?
What kinds of evidence are stronger for identifying an anonymous author: manuscript clues, dates, vocabulary, or shared doctrines?
Can a distinction between types of propositions solve a puzzle without committing the writer to unusual claims about nonexistent things?

summaries.example: Suppose a friend says, “All the players are one team.” This can mean that every player belongs to the same team, or it can sound as if all the players are literally one person. The words have been put together in a confusing way. A good solver would give a reason for one reading, a reason against another reading, and then explain which meaning changed. Richard used this kind of step-by-step method with sentences such as “Every man is every man.”
summaries.summary: Richard the Sophister was a thirteenth-century English philosopher and logician associated with Oxford. His work Abstractiones gathered more than three hundred sentences called sophisms. A sophism is a reasoning puzzle: it may look easy, but a word, phrase, or sentence pattern creates competing interpretations. The collection examines logical expressions such as “all,” “every,” “or,” “if,” “and,” “not,” “except,” “necessary,” and “possible.” Richard’s first example, “Every man is every man,” can be supported if “every man” means each man separately. It can be rejected if the same phrase is taken to mean all men together. The solution is that the phrase is being used in two different ways. Richard’s summaries generally present the puzzle, arguments supporting it, arguments opposing it, and a final explanation of the fallacy. The book was probably written around the 1230s or 1240s and became a useful text in medieval education. Several manuscripts survive, but the identity of their author is still uncertain. Scholars have proposed different men named Richard, yet the evidence does not prove one identification.
key_ideas: Richard’s Abstractiones contains over three hundred logic puzzles and was likely used as a teaching handbook.
Many puzzles are difficult because a word can have different meanings or because sentence structure changes what belongs with what.
Richard’s method compares arguments on both sides before naming the fallacy and explaining the solution.
The book was known in medieval university circles and survives through several manuscripts, including incomplete and derivative copies.
The author’s name was Richard, but historians disagree about which Richard he was.
summaries.why_it_matters: These puzzles teach an important habit: before deciding whether an argument is correct, check what its words mean in that particular sentence. The entry also shows how historical knowledge is built from incomplete evidence. Researchers must compare manuscripts, dates, language, and ideas, while keeping their conclusions appropriately cautious.

important_terms.definition: A tricky sentence used to test reasoning, often because its words or grammar allow more than one interpretation.
A person who studies valid reasoning. In the medieval setting of this entry, “sophista” meant a logician, not simply someone who tries to fool people.
A reasoning mistake, such as using one word in two different senses without noticing.
A phrase or word that changes how a whole sentence works, such as “all,” “if,” “or,” or “not.”
A question-setting or imagined situation used to give a sophism its context.
A structured medieval classroom debate in which a claim was supported, challenged, and resolved.

questions_to_think_about: How can a sentence seem true under one interpretation and false under another?
Why might a teacher ask students to argue both for and against a claim?
What is the difference between a confusing sentence and a false sentence?
Why is it risky to identify an author using only similar vocabulary or ideas?
Which modern arguments might depend on the meanings of words like “all,” “only,” or “if”?
